source_refs.note: Book p. 56: 2.11 Local Linear Approximation (Linearization), introduction before 2.11.1

blocks.text: Sometimes, complicated functions are hard to work with, so we use simpler functions to approximate them. These approximations are often accurate enough for practical purposes.
In this section, we discuss linearization, which uses tangent lines to approximate a function near a specific point.

Linearization simplifies complex or nonlinear functions with a straight-line approximation, making calculations easier. It is widely used in machine learning, physics, engineering, and economics for quick, local estimates, especially for small changes around known values.

The whole idea in one picture: zoom in very close to a point on a smooth curve and the curve looks almost straight. That almost-straight piece is the tangent line at the point. A straight line is easy to calculate with (only multiplying and adding), so near the point we use the tangent line in place of the curve.
What you already need: the derivative \(f'(a)\) is the slope of the tangent at \(x = a\), and a line through \((a, f(a))\) with slope \(m\) is \(y = f(a) + m(x - a)\). Linearization (2.11.1) puts these two facts together.
Typical use: values such as \(\sqrt{9.2}\), \(\sqrt[3]{82}\) or \(\cos 91^\circ\) are hard by hand, but \(\sqrt{9}\), \(\sqrt[3]{64}\) and \(\cos 90^\circ\) are easy. We start at the easy value and let the tangent line carry us a small step to the hard one.
blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text:
1. A complicated function can be replaced near a point by a simpler one: its tangent line.
2. The approximation is local: good only for \(x\) close to the chosen point.
3. The closer \(x\) is to the point, the better the estimate; far away it can be poor.
4. Linearization is used for quick estimates in science, engineering and economics.
blocks.title: Key points

blocks.text:
1. Thinking the tangent-line value is exact. It is an approximation; write \(\approx\), not \(=\).
2. Using a tangent line far from its point of contact: the curve bends away and the error grows.
